articles.title: Influencers are supposed to influence us – so why are they asking us what they should do?
articles.author: Catherine Greenwood, Lecturer in Digital Marketing, University of Lancashire
paras: An influencer posts a photograph of two designer handbags and asks her followers which one she should buy. Another wants recommendations for restaurants in a new city she is visiting. Someone else asks which beauty dupes are actually worth trying.

These are ordinary questions we might ask our friends. Yet, coming from people who have built careers influencing what others buy, wear and desire, they raise an interesting question. If influencers are supposed to influence their followers, why are they increasingly asking them what they should do? The answer may be that asking for advice may not mean giving up influence at all, but another way for influencers to maintain it.

In my doctoral research, I analysed 390 Instagram posts from three established luxury fashion influencers. I examined how they communicated identity, aspiration and authenticity through images, captions and other visual messaging.

One observation was the use of questions within captions, inviting followers to respond to content that was otherwise carefully constructed. A polished fashion photograph might be accompanied by conversational language, encouraging audiences to engage with the person behind the image.

These interactions interested me because they demonstrated how influencers could communicate exclusivity and accessibility simultaneously. They might be attending prestigious fashion events or wearing expensive clothing, yet their captions created opportunities for seemingly ordinary conversation.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today
Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption
The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you

Asking followers for recommendations takes this a little further. There is a difference between asking people what they think of an outfit and inviting them to help make a decision. Followers are no longer simply responding to someone else’s taste, but being invited to contribute their own.

This is particularly interesting in fashion, where influence has traditionally been associated with possessing knowledge, recognising desirable things and communicating taste to others. Yet here we have people who possess considerable fashion authority apparently seeking that judgment from their audiences.
The performance of being approachable

In his influential book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959), sociologist Erving Goffman argued that people manage how they present themselves to others, adjusting their behaviour according to the impressions they wish to communicate.
This offers a useful way of understanding influencer culture, where seemingly informal moments can contribute to a carefully maintained public identity.

A homeware influencer might genuinely need advice about blinds. But asking also communicates something about them. It presents them as approachable, interested in other people’s experiences and willing to admit that they do not already know everything.
Importantly, none of these qualities requires an influencer to surrender the authority that made people follow them in the first place.

Media scholar Crystal Abidin describes this relationship through the concept of perceived interconnectedness. This describes the interactions that create a sense of familiarity and mutual connection between influencers and their audiences.

Unlike traditional celebrities, whose audiences largely watch from a distance, influencers operate within platforms that allow followers to speak back. Being asked for advice can deepen this sense of connection. There is a particular satisfaction in feeling that somebody whose life you follow might be interested in your opinion.
Who is actually influencing whom?

Of course, followers may genuinely shape an influencer’s decisions. Someone might recommend an unfamiliar designer, an independent restaurant or a product that subsequently appears in their content. It would be misleading to suggest that every question is a calculated attempt to generate engagement. But participation does not necessarily mean equal influence.

The influencer decides what to ask, which recommendations to acknowledge and whether to act on them. The audience may contribute the knowledge, but the influencer retains considerable control over how that knowledge is selected and presented.

This is where the blinds example is particularly interesting. The influencer’s followers might possess knowledge about suppliers, materials or products that she does not. Yet she retains the authority to decide what fits the aesthetic identity she has established. There is, after all, a difference between knowing where to buy something and knowing how to make it desirable.

When an influencer publicly adopts a follower’s recommendation, that choice can become influential in its own right. What began as somebody else’s advice becomes part of the influencer’s communication of taste.
This challenges the idea that influence simply travels in one direction. Instead, audiences can participate in producing the knowledge and cultural references that influencers subsequently share.

For fashion brands and marketers, this matters because an influencer’s value may lie not only in their ability to recommend products, but also in their ability to make audiences feel involved in the process through which recommendations acquire meaning.

Perhaps we have become so accustomed to influencers telling us what to buy that we overlook what happens when they ask us instead. The apparent reversal can make the relationship feel less hierarchical, without necessarily changing who holds the greatest authority.

articles.title: I’m an artist who works with glass – here’s how the physics and chemistry of glassblowing work
articles.author: Suzanne Peck, Lecturer of Art, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive and demanding.

When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel and to find some focus within and among the kinetic.

The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability.

At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass. This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius).

In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass. You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave.

Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid, meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point. Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range.
Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working.

We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed.

When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone – probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid.

To make anything – a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb or a pumpkin – you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions.

You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability, allowing you to continue working it without breaking it.

A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times.

Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone.

So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object – utilitarian, domestic and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete.

Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin.

I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years.

I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly.

If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer: a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C).

This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours.

As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble – the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on.

The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky.

articles.title: Centuries before TikTok, this 1579 bestseller gave readers their daily dose of ‘brain rot’
articles.author: James Fox, Research Associate in the School of Modern Languages and Cultures, University of Glasgow
paras: First you are shown a new hack to keep wine from spoiling. Then a dog lovingly devoted to its owner. Immediately in tow there are methods to repair broken glass and remove acne, a tip for weight loss, a cake recipe and an astrological reading of your future. But this is not your TikTok or Instagram feed – it’s the contents of a book written nearly four-and-a-half centuries ago.

The English writer Thomas Lupton’s book A Thousand Notable Things was first published in 1579. True to its title, it collected roughly 1,000 short passages ordered randomly, one after another. A seemingly endless stream of household “life hacks”, sensational stories and recipes, it offered answers for just about everything.

Trouble sleeping? Rub your forehead with a mix of white poppy and henbane seeds. If you find yourself bewitched, leave a mercury-filled quill under your pillow. And have you heard the folklore that claims when a robin red breast finds a dead human, they cover its face in moss?

Flitting through eclectic, attention-grabbing short-form content may be the de facto mode of media consumption in the 21st century. But how-to books like A Thousand Notable Things suggest that our ancestors’ preoccupations were not entirely different.

Lupton understood the wide appeal of such easily digestible material. In a revealing preface, he argued that imbibing many passages of “strangeness and variety” was preferable to being “fed too long with one food” by reading entire books.

It proved a winning formula. A Thousand Notable Things enjoyed at least 33 editions, remaining in print from the time Sir Francis Drake was circumnavigating the globe until 1827, the year the first known photograph was taken.
Its success belonged to a burgeoning taste for “books of secrets”, recipe-like instructional texts that taught everything from cosmetics and alchemy to brewing and beekeeping.

Originating in Italy, and published throughout the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, the most popular of these works were continually translated and reprinted throughout Europe. They are now recognised as exerting genuine influence on contemporary scientific culture.

Whether providing alchemical routes to the philosopher’s stone or the recipe for a nutritious stew, books like A Thousand Notable Things thrived on the promise of revealing hidden “secrets” about nature’s inner workings.

Of course, there was no guarantee that everything Lupton suggested would work: whether sleeping on your right side during pregnancy really meant the baby would be female, or that dreaming of eagles flying overhead was necessarily a sign of imminent good fortune. Sheer efficacy alone wasn’t the point. The appeal lay in the wonder, curiosity and amusement that accompanied practical instruction.

If some passages sound absurd or downright dangerous to modern ears (henbane and mercury are highly poisonous), consider that much of Lupton’s material was cutting-edge in its day. His most cited source was Antoine Mizauld, a Parisian medical professor and advisor to French queen Marguerite de Valois.
Even though the vitality of astrology, occult science and ancient medicine waned over the book’s 250-year lifespan, the deeply human concerns it addressed proved enduringly popular.
We know that contemporary readers found Lupton’s eclectic material engaging thanks to their annotations in personal copies, precious few of which remain today.

One survivor from 1612, now in the Glasgow University Library, is marked with small crosses at passages on lameness, heart trouble, ulcers, meat eating and stomach problems. We might speculate that its owner was managing symptoms of dietary issues or gout. So too are gout cures underlined in a copy owned by the 17th-century book collector Frances Wolfreston.
Another reader pencilled crosses next to 38 predominantly medical passages in their 1706 copy, including remedies for head and toothaches, burning eyes, shortness of breath, sore throat and insomnia.

Others were more selective. One copy in the Wellcome Collection is marked only occasionally, including at an anecdote about a German farmer who died with terrible pain in his side. A surgeon cut him open to find large pieces of wood and four steel knives, afflictions that were blamed on the Devil.

Just as we worry today about the pernicious effects of TikTok, 16th-century commentators also feared the “brain-rotting” potential of low-brow mass entertainment, distraction and information overload.

But Lupton’s take was more optimistic. Offering bite-size morsels gleaned from a wide range of texts, in plain English rather than scholarly Latin, gave ordinary readers access to knowledge that otherwise required whole libraries to attain.

These how to books, which are the subject of an ongoing research collaboration between Glasgow University and the Herzog August library in Germany, will take centre stage in an exhibition at the Mitchell Library, Glasgow, from January to March 2027.

Whether or not they are direct antecedents of today’s instructional media, these texts encapsulate both the past’s profound strangeness, and those facets of human experience that seem perennial: the potent dialectic of similarity and difference that makes history so compelling. If nothing else, they might provide a handy hack to stave off your next headache.

articles.title: Ernest Shackleton turned a major disappointment in the Antarctic into fame back in Britain
articles.author: Ed Armston-Sheret, Fellow at the Institute of Historical Research, School of Advanced Study, University of London
paras: Ernest Shackleton is one of the most well-known polar explorers in history. He’s mostly remembered for his incredible leadership following the sinking of his ship Endurance in the Weddell Sea in November 1915, which saved his life and the 27 others on board.

Yet had you known Shackleton in 1895, his future fame as an Antarctic explorer would have seemed highly unlikely. At the time, he was an unknown officer in the merchant navy, and Antarctica meant little to him. He had never even put on a pair of skis.

So how did Shackleton become such a famous polar explorer? This is one of the questions at the heart of my book The Grip of the Ice and the answer is suprising: his fame had as much to do with what he did back home as it did with his time on the ice.

Shackleton’s polar career started with the British National Antarctic Expedition, usually known as the Discovery Expedition (named after its ship). The venture was jointly organised by the Royal Geographical Society and the Royal Society and partly funded by the government. The gregarious Shackleton found a place on the expedition by befriending Cedric Longstaff, the son of one of the expedition’s major donors. On the March 15 1901, Shackleton was ordered to report to the Discovery’s commander, Robert Falcon Scott, at the expedition’s office in Mayfair. He would be the ship’s third lieutenant.

Arriving in Antarctica in January 1902, they explored the continent’s coast and then spent the winter on board their ship in McMurdo Sound. During the months of polar darkness, conditions were too harsh for further exploration. Shackleton became a vital and well-liked member of the Discovery expedition. To help keep up morale while cooped up on board the ship, he edited The South Polar Times – the first magazine ever published in Antarctica.

Shackleton soon heard exciting news: Scott had selected him, along with the expedition’s zoologist and junior medic Edward Wilson, to accompany him on a journey towards the South Pole. This would be the expedition’s first major journey.

Leaving the ship on November 2 1902, the journey started off well, with Siberian huskies helping to pull the men’s sledges. They were soon further south than any explorers before them. But things gradually began to unravel. The dogs weakened due to problems with their food, the men grew hungry on insufficient supplies and they couldn’t move their sledges forward all st once, drastically reducing their daily distances.

Shackleton and Scott may also have had an argument on this journey, with Albert Armitage, the expedition’s second in command, later suggesting in his letters that Scott called Shackleton a “bloody fool” during a heated argument. Even so, they patched things up and trudged southwards. Eventually, they managed to lighten their sledges by leaving supplies for the return march in a depot, improving their rate of progress. However, their dogs continued to weaken so Shackleton and Wilson killed the sickest animals and fed them to the stronger ones.

By Christmas 1902, the men were also in trouble. Wilson inspected the men’s gums and noticed signs of scurvy – a disease we now know is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Soon, they were forced to turn back, having achieved a new furthest south record of around 480 miles from the South Pole on December 31 1902.

On the march back to the ship, Shackleton’s health deteriorated rapidly. As well as suffering from scurvy, he was also coughing up blood. When the last of their dogs was killed, Scott and Wilson pulled the sledge while Shackleton made painful progress on skis.
Eventually, on February 3 1903, they got back to the ship to find that the Morning, a relief vessel, had arrived.

The Discovery was still trapped in the ice and, with winter closing in, Scott ordered that Shackleton return to New Zealand when the Morning sailed northwards on March 2 1903. Among polar historians, Scott’s decision has been controversial. Some suggest that Scott saw Shackleton as a potential rival, though there isn’t a great deal of evidence for this.
Early return and celebrity

So, Shackleton’s career as a polar explorer seemed to have got off to a bad start. While Scott sent him back with a glowing reference, he had been pronounced unfit for further Antarctic exploration. Frustratingly, he seemed “practically well” according to Gerald S Doorly, then a junior officer on the Morning, by the time he arrived in New Zealand and was in even better shape when he reached London.
Shackleton’s diaries show that he felt a mix of emotions: frustration, embarrassment and disappointment. He had been desperate to stay another winter and see the expedition through to its finish.
Yet studying this period, what amazed me was how Shackleton took advantage of his early return to Britain.

As the only officer back from Antarctica, he was in a unique position to tell the public and the media what had happened on their journey. He wrote articles for The Illustrated London News and Pearson’s Magazine and gave lectures to enthralled audiences, eager to hear about his amazing journey towards the South Pole.

Shackleton was also involved in equipping a relief vessel, the Dundee whaler Terra Nova, to help free the explorers from the ice the following year. By early 1904, he’d even managed to land a job as secretary of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society.

The Discovery expedition transformed Shackleton from an unknown officer in the Merchant Navy into one of the best-known polar explorers in Britain. He’d also built a wealth of logistical experience and connections that left him perfectly placed to launch an expedition of his own – which he did in 1907, much to Scott’s annoyance.
In his return to London, Shackleton had demonstrated his unique ability to make the very best of a disaster.

articles.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
articles.author: Michelle Comber, Lecturer in Archaeology, School of Geography, Archaeology and Irish Studies, University of Galway
paras: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portrays medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there’s little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

Leisure activities are often overlooked, despite the fact that they existed in one form or another at most – if not all – levels of medieval society. The intangible nature of much of the evidence, often coupled with poor preservation of physical objects, can help explain this.

However, when conditions are right, archaeological remains can shed light on the extra-curricular activities of medieval folk. My colleagues and I found abundant evidence of life’s luxuries at the site of Caherconnell Cashel in the Burren region of western Ireland.

Caherconnell Cashel was a farmstead of houses and workshops enclosed within a well-preserved circular dry stone wall. Such settlements are also known as ringforts and generally housed a single family (possibly multiple generations). Caherconnell was a large ringfort; the home of wealthy local rulers from the late 10th century AD to the early 17th century. Our recently concluded excavations revealed all aspects of life at this well-preserved family settlement.

While activities such as fighting, farming, industry and crafts were clearly represented in material recovered from the site, so too were the less mundane activities of game playing, literacy, and music.

The true extent of game playing is undoubtedly lost in the perishable nature of the materials used extensively in such pursuits – such as wood, leather and textiles. At Caherconnell, however, surviving evidence includes small gaming pieces made of bone and antler, metal, clay and stone.

One of the more complete finds was an 11th-century barrel-shaped and polished antler gaming piece. A bronze peg or stem runs through its hollow core and projects from its base. It originally had a plate or cap at the top, the loss of which may have resulted in the piece being discarded or set aside for repair.

Pegged game pieces like this were used in the Saxon and Viking board game of hnefatafl, a game that appeared in Ireland around the 9th or 10th century AD. Hnefatafl, and other games like it, provided both strategy training and entertainment.

Evidence of literacy at Caherconnell includes writing implements and associated equipment. One of our most remarkable finds was an 11th-century pen made from bone and bronze. The slender hollow bone shaft or barrel was probably made from the bone of a wader bird or swan.

Experimental work by the archaeologist Adam Parsons found that the closest match was a swan radius (a tubular bone) from the right-side wing. Inserted into the narrow end of the barrel is a tapering bronze point or nib.

The Caherconnell pen finds no exact comparisons within Ireland or elsewhere; its early secular context is also, so far, unique. Until now, evidence of early literacy in Ireland has been largely confined to monastic and related church sites. At Caherconnell, the pen may have been used in general record keeping and external communications.

However, it also reminds us that literate occupants of Caherconnell Cashel may have enjoyed composing, reading, and sharing ancestral pedigrees, praise poetry and epic tales “of gods and fighting men”.
The musical sounds of a settlement are rarely represented in its archaeological record. Wood, a common material in the construction of various instruments, rarely survives to the present day.

Metal and bone fittings, however, have been found during excavations, including at Caherconnell, where bone and bronze tuning pegs were among the finds. Two of the tuning pegs are readily identifiable as components of stringed instruments.

They have a circular sectioned shaft that splays slightly into a rectangular sectioned turning block at one end (now missing from the larger bone example). The opposite end pinches in slightly and is perforated by a small circular hole through which the string was attached.
The bone tuning peg, being a relatively soft material, still bears impressions from the wire-string of the instrument. Both date to the 11th century, but they are clearly from different instruments.
One had strong bronze pegs, the other had larger bone versions. Outside Ireland, shorter tuning pegs are commonly associated with lyres, lutes and fiddles (up to 65mm is classed as short).

No lutes or fiddles survive from early Ireland, however. Nor are there any written references to, or depictions of them. The lyre, on the other hand, is represented. Depictions are found in several ecclesiastical contexts and early Irish literature confirms that lyres or lyre-like instruments were also used outside religious settings.

Music, and accompanying songs and poetry, probably fulfilled various social, political, and cultural functions. These range from proclaiming the magnificence of the nobility to entertaining a family around their hearth in the evening.

Life at Caherconnell was, in many ways, very traditional. It was a place where ancestry and heritage were valued, yet it was also a place connected to the outside world. In leisure, as in so many other facets of their lives, the occupants encountered, adopted, and no doubt adapted the most desirable elements of a wider cultural realm.

It is clear from this one site that those with more leisure time, often the wealthier in society, filled that time with various recreational pursuits. However, human nature suggests that all classes engaged in such activities, albeit often in a manner that’s less visible to archaeologists.

After all, you didn’t need a fancy bronze and antler game set to play games, writing equipment to create stories, or peg-tuned wired instruments to compose and sing a song. Such things just prove the existence of these activities, not how commonplace they were.

The Caherconnell excavations were funded by the Caherconnell Archaeology Field School, and some of its post-excavation analyses by Ireland's National Monuments Service via a Royal Irish Academy research-excavation grant.

articles.title: The surprising origins of Denmark’s reputation for open-mindedness
articles.author: Detlef Siegfried, Professor of Modern German and European History, University of Copenhagen
paras: Ask Danes what makes Denmark Danish and you might hear about openness, tolerance and the freedom to live as you choose.

You can see it in the country’s history: Denmark was the first country in the world to legalise pornography. Alternative communities such as Christiania in Copenhagen are internationally famous for their counterculture and liberal attitudes. And Danish activists have helped push ideas about sexuality and family life in new directions.
But there is a less obvious part of this story.
Denmark did not develop its reputation for open-mindedness entirely on its own. Some of the people who helped create that image were looking at Denmark from across the border.

From the 1960s onwards, West Germany became an important audience for Denmark’s emerging reputation as a more liberal society. For young Germans frustrated with what they saw as a conservative, hierarchical and authoritarian society, Denmark looked like a place where people had more freedom to experiment with different ways of living.

West Germany in the 1960s and 1970s was still grappling with the legacy of Nazism. Many young people in the West German New Left rejected the social and political values of their parents’ generation and looked for alternatives.
The situation was also different across the German divide. In East Germany, the communist state offered its own very different model of society and controlled many aspects of public and private life.
For young West Germans seeking alternatives, Denmark seemed like something else entirely: a nearby democratic country where social experimentation seemed possible.

Research I am carrying out with my colleague Tobias Haimin de Fønss Wung-Sung into West German reactions to Denmark during this period shows how several aspects of Danish life contributed to this image.

Christiania, the self-governing community in Copenhagen, became associated with communal living and alternative lifestyles. The New Left political movement challenged established politics and social norms. Roskilde music festival grew into an important gathering place for young people and counterculture. Denmark also experimented with progressive approaches to education and pornography.
From abroad, this created an image of Denmark as a country where people were unusually free to live differently.

In 1969, when the Danish parliament legalised pornographic images , its decision was highly controversial among Danes. But it attracted considerable attention internationally, particularly in West Germany, where the new government under Chancellor Willy Brandt prepared a similar reform.
The result was not simply a change in Danish law. People, products and money began moving across the border.

Government officials travelled to Copenhagen to learn about the effects of the liberalisation. West Germans travelled to Denmark to buy pornography. Danish producers gained access to a much larger market south of the border. Denmark could even be imagined in West Germany as a kind of porn paradise.
Our research into West German reactions to Denmark’s liberalisation between 1965 and 1985 shows how the country became associated with a new kind of sexual freedom.

Danish homosexual people and activists also developed connections with larger gay communities in West Germany, particularly in Berlin and Hamburg. And Denmark developed its own naturist culture, not least inspired by the German movement of freikörperkultur (pronounced FRY-kur-per-kul-toor) or “free body culture”. People gathered to swim, sunbathe and socialise naked.
People, ideas and practices were therefore moving in both directions across the border.
Reputation and national values
Over time, these developments helped turn Denmark’s reputation for social liberalism into something more than an international image. It became part of how Denmark could describe itself.

In 2016, for example, the Danish government asked the public to identify values considered particularly important to Danish society. The resulting Danmarkskanon, or Danish Canon, included ten such values. One was frisind (pronounced free-sin) – a word that can mean open-mindedness, tolerance or freedom from conventional moral constraints.

The Canon described frisind in terms of openness towards traditional moral ideas, the body and sexuality. It pointed to Denmark’s relaxed attitude towards nudity, tolerance of different forms of family and sexual life, alternative lifestyles and the legalisation of pornography.

By this point, what had once been a contested and internationally shaped reputation had become something that could be presented as part of Denmark’s cultural heritage. But that does not necessarily mean Danes have always been uniquely tolerant.

The Danish criminologist Berl Kutchinsky (1935-1995) studied the liberalisation of pornography extensively and he was sceptical of precisely this idea. He argued that Denmark’s exceptional liberalism was something of a myth.

In his view, Danes still belonged to the broadly “puritanical, post-Victorian” family of European nations. Denmark was simply among the less puritanical members of that group, alongside Sweden, the Netherlands and Germany. Compared with them, he considered Danes “slightly more liberal and permissive” when it came to sexuality.
If Kutchinsky was right, Danish frisind is less about being uniquely liberal than about being liberal in comparison with particular neighbours.
The history of Danish frisind therefore stretches well beyond Denmark.

And while it has been shaped by changing laws and attitudes inside the country, people travelling across the border, activists building international networks and products finding new markets have also played a role.
That is easy to lose sight of once an idea becomes part of a national identity.

The Danish Canon presents frisind as a Danish value. But its history suggests something more complicated: Denmark’s reputation for open-mindedness was, at least partly, made through its relationships with other countries.
In other words, one of the very things Denmark considers particularly Danish likely started out more as a comparison with somewhere else.

articles.title: The Odyssey’s sea monsters are terrifying expressions of ‘ecohorror’
articles.author: Ryan Denson, Honorary Research Fellow, University of Exeter; University of Silesia in Katowice
paras: The ancient Greeks are generally thought of as a people at home on the sea. Yet their familiarity with the ocean didn’t stop them from fearing it. Danger and uncertainty always loomed over ancient voyages, and this is reflected in writing from the time.

One of the most famous works of ancient Greek literature is, after all, a poem about a man lost at sea for a decade. Homer’s Odyssey is famed for its many monsters, some of which can be read as what scholars have dubbed “ecohorror” – expressions of human fears of the natural world.

Monsters themselves are often more than mere misapprehensions of real animals or natural forces. They can be creative “what ifs” – imaginative extrapolations of background cultural fears. The first of the Odyssey’s two main sea monsters, Charybdis, is what initially seems to be a creature causing a gigantic whirlpool, yet the Odyssey hints at another particularly unsettling quality. As Odysseus describes the encounter:

We sailed out into the strait, lamenting, for Scylla was on this side, and on the other was Charybdis; dreadfully she sucked down the briny sea water. Whenever she vomited forth again, like a cauldron in a large fire, all boiled over and stirred up, foam fell from above onto the peaks of both cliffs. But when she sucked down the briny sea water, from within she was revealed all stirred up, and roared dreadfully all about the rock, and the ground appeared underneath with dark-blue sand, and pale-green fear took hold of us.

Here, we are told that the whirlpool sucks in so much water that the sailors actually seem to glimpse inside. While the poem states that “she was revealed”, Odysseus sees not a monstrous entity, but only the sea floor itself.

This eerie absence of physical form – itself immediately followed by the detail of the fear felt by Odysseus and his crew – highlights that Charybdis is an entirely disembodied figure. She’s not a physical creature dwelling beneath the waves but an animate, hungry stretch of ocean itself.
This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

Ecohorror expresses itself here with the enmeshment of a monster with the environment itself by making a monster out of the environment itself. But, rather than being a monster causing a whirlpool, Charybdis is better understood as a monstrous patch of water – a potentially living portion of the environment itself, and one that sparks terror in humans.

Across the strait from Charybdis is Scylla. Whereas Charybdis eerily lacks form altogether, part of Scylla’s monstrosity stems from her grotesque body. The poem describes her as having 12 feet, six throats and three rows of teeth in each mouth. It’s a description that anticipates grotesque and unfathomable nature of some modern monsters like those of H. P. Lovecraft.
Yet ecohorror expresses itself, not through Scylla’s monstrous form, but in the way that she attacks. As Odysseus describes:

We gazed at [Charybdis], fearing destruction, meanwhile Scylla snatched six of my comrades from the hollow of the ship, those who were the best with their hands and fighting. Looking back on the ship, I perceived only the hands and feet of my companions as they were pulled upwards … Scylla devoured them as they screamed and stretched out their hands to me in their horrid struggle.
The swiftness with which Odysseus’ crew members are hoisted into the air paints an especially vivid scene.
Terror is marked by their lamentable screams. Ecohorror here lies in the poet’s explicit inversion of the conventional human engagement with the marine environment.

It is, of course, normally fishermen that prey on marine life, hauling them upward on fishing lines to be taken as food. Yet, in this space below Scylla’s cliff-side abode, humans have themselves become the prey for a more fearsome predator of the marine world, to be “fished up” and devoured themselves.

Of course, no ancient Greek ever encountered any marine dangers on the exaggerated scale of the threats posed by Scylla and Charybdis. But this did not hinder creative and imaginative cultural expressions of what could be encountered by a wayward sailor.

Episodes such as these in Homer’s Odyssey capture and develop the uncertainties surrounding ancient sea travel, from the fear of what might lurk beneath the waves to the anxiety of becoming prey to a marine creature.

As part of the Rethinking the Classics series, we’re asking our experts to recommend a book or artwork that tackles similar themes to the canonical work in question, but isn’t (yet) considered a classic itself. Here is Ryan Denson’s suggestion:

Nobody alive today can claim firsthand knowledge of what it felt like to navigate the open Mediterranean in the ancient world, nor the sheer terror it inspired. While marine monsters are not unknown in modern literature, ecohorror does tend to take on other forms, derived from our own experiences of nature.

Mexican Gothic (2020) by Mexican-Canadian author Silvia Moreno-Garcia is a good example. This novel follows Noemí Taboada, who is venturing to a rural mansion to check up on her cousin, recently married off to one of its inhabitants. Noemí ultimately discovers that the house is haunted, not by ghosts, but by a sentient fungus psychically controlling the aristocratic family living there.

Moreno-Garcia’s tale is an ecohorror based on modern fears. None of us have ever encountered a house controlled by a malevolent supernatural fungus. But we all have felt the sudden dread at discovering a spot of mould growing in our home, and the fear that it might spread, or may already linger elsewhere. Ecohorror in Mexican Gothic, as in the Odyssey, serves as a genre to explore creative “what if” scenarios extrapolated from everyday experiences and anxieties.

articles.title: La Bola Negra: this deeply moving cinematic homage to Lorca is part of his queer legacy
articles.author: Santiago Fouz Hernández, Professor in the School of Modern Languages and Cultures, Durham University
paras: Directed by legendary Spanish film-making duo Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – also known as “Los Javis” – La Bola Negra (The Black Ball) is Spain’s big hope for next year’s Oscars.

The film reimagines the unfinished 1936 work of the same name by the Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca (1898-1936), based on the only four existing pages. It would have been Lorca’s first play with a gay protagonist.

La bola negra is also co-written by Los Javis in collaboration with queer playwright Alberto Conejero, author of the original play La Piedra Oscura (The Dark Stone, 2013) on which the film is also partly based.

The film’s title refers to Lorca’s original story, in which Carlos, a young gay man (Milo Quifes) tries and fails to join a private club due to rumours about his sexuality. The selection committee votes in secret, using white and black balls. The black ones represent rejection – hence the term “blackballed” – and, implicitly, social exclusion.

Los Javis first became well known for three major streaming series: the hilarious Paquita Salas (Netflix 2020), a tragicomic story about a has-been talent agent; Veneno (HBO Max, 2020), based on the life of a trans sex worker who became a national celebrity in 1990s Spain; and the ambitious religious musical drama La Mesías (MUBI, 2023).

It is hard to believe that La Bola Negra is only their second feature, after La llamada (Holy Camp, 2017), their hugely successful musical about a lesbian romance. This new film is a significant leap in scale, production values and global reach.

After La Bola Negra’s triumph at Cannes, where Los Javis won best direction, the film also won audience awards at San Sebastián, Toronto and London, drawing full houses on the festival circuit. It also quickly became a social media phenomenon and has been acquired by Netflix.
Federico García Lorca and queer history
Lorca, considered Spain’s most influential 20th-century poet and playwright, was executed by firing squad in 1936, at the start of the Spanish civil war, because of his politics and sexuality.

In the film, Lorca’s unfinished text is a seed that grows and expands into the 21st century, pausing at three moments in Spain’s history: the second republic in 1932, the civil war in 1937, and contemporary Spain in 2017, taking in three gay stories.

In the second story, based on Conejero’s play, Lorca’s real-life lover Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau) is a Republican prisoner of war. He develops a fleeting platonic infatuation for his Nationalist guard, Sebastián, played brilliantly by popular singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente in his first acting role.

Their connection becomes part of a complex chain of relationships and revelations that carries the story – and queer history – forward, aided by an enveloping score by Raül Refree and exquisite cinematography by Gris Jordana.

Lorca’s legacy runs through the film, explicitly through his unfinished play, his homoerotic sketches, and even his presence depicted in a small cameo (Alberto Cortés). More implicitly, it is evoked through the dramatic Spanish settings and the depiction of motherhood, a subject he examined extensively in his work.

Lola Dueñas gives a remarkable supporting performance as Teresa, a troubled single mother. Penélope Cruz’s stellar performance as a glamorous cabaret singer includes one of the film’s most memorable lines, while Glenn Close plays an American Lorca scholar entirely in Spanish.

The film is packed with queer imagery across time. These range from a war-torn statue of the persecuted Saint Sebastian, who has become a contemporary queer-icon, to hypermasculine sailor figures reminiscent of German film-maker Rainer Werner Fassbinder’s classic homoerotic film Querelle, to the unmistakable gay dating app Grindr.

Shot on 35mm film, La Bola Negra seamlessly combines moments of great drama and intense intimacy in relatively small spaces that contrast with landscapes of epic proportions. Jordana’s lush cinematography gives the movie a consistent look throughout, while creating a distinctive ambience for each of the three story parts.

The film’s queer gaze embraces both ideals of masculinity and body diversity. Alongside the taut bodies of the characters played by heartthrobs Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente, the protagonist of the final section is Alberto, a larger-bodied gay man played by Carlos González. Famous for his queer roles in streaming hits such as Veneno (2020), and Mariliendre (Fag Hag, 2025), González delivers another standout performance, while adding important elements of body and sex positivity to the story.

Queer people have long been excluded from official histories: ignored, silenced or presented in ways that obscure their sexuality. In repressive societies, invisibility is a matter of survival, shaped by internalised homophobia and imposed closets. La Bola Negra makes that history visible, while celebrating the role queer people play in shaping culture: Lorca as a playwright, Sebastián as a musician, Alberto as a queer historian.

That reclamation has resonance in today’s Spain, a country often associated with LGBTQ+ progress. The third country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage in 2005, Spain currently ranks first in Europe on the 2026 Rainbow Map for legal rights and protections, yet the political climate feels increasingly uncertain.

Francoist and fascist nostalgia is finding new audiences through social media, even among young people, and the possibility of a conservative and far-right coalition hangs over Spain’s general election on November 29. As cultural historian Nicholas Manganas has argued, the film’s return to Spain’s past feels strikingly connected to the present.

Lorca’s remains are still believed to lie in an unmarked mass grave in his native province of Granada. His unfinished manuscript, however, survives as a symbol of queer legacy and inheritance. In the film, its pages become a baton passed across generations. But they are also an emblem of reparation for the queer shame, represented in the film by the black ball of the title, and its symbolic weight in Lorca’s original 1936 story.

By bringing the Spanish poet and playwright’s story back to life through an predominantly queer cast in a production that is heavy with queer iconography, Los Javis make La Bola Negra part of the very legacy their film seeks to reclaim.
Santiago Fouz Hernández receives funding from the British Academy. He is affiliated with the Spanish Government as Honorary Vice Consul of Spain for the North East and Cumbria.

articles.title: What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan
articles.author: Christopher A. Snyder, PhD, Professor of History, Mississippi State University
paras: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project, an adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried. In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he really look like David Bowie, with the voice of Meryl Streep?

For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: He is a representation of Jesus. Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “Chronicles of Narnia,” which have sold over 120 million copies worldwide since the series’ publication in the 1950s.

As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and “Lord of the Rings” author J.R.R. Tolkien, who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself was a medievalist at Oxford, and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology.
Both authors acknowledged the ethical and religious themes of their fiction. Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory.

“The Magician’s Nephew,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.”

Later in the series, Aslan sacrifices himself to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.

Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like Philip Pullman, who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda.”

Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a famous late-night conversation with Tolkien in September 1931.

The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to accept Christianity as the “true myth.”

Almost immediately, Lewis began writing Christian apologetics, intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.
But what did Lewis himself say about Aslan?
His letters and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be allegorical. In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.
Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”

Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis wrote in a 1958 letter. “This is not allegory at all.”

Neither Lewis nor Tolkien approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was not simply the product of the author and their time, a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning.

And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “The Allegory of Love” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “The Pilgrim’s Regress” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.

Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “Leaf by Niggle” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “The Lord of the Rings.” Like his earlier novel “The Hobbit,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.

Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later wrote to one schoolgirl.

“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “The Allegory of Love,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real.

For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.

In 2018, the author’s estate sold Netflix the rights to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” and has generally been enthusiastic about the project.

Gerwig herself has expressed her “reverence” for Lewis’ work. “It was the book of my childhood,” she said at a press event in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”

Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with her film “Little Women,” Gerwig is adapting a beloved novel. And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have inspired the faith of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.

Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the medieval and Renaissance literature that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.

articles.title: AI won’t ever make a historically accurate film – but it could help archaeology create better stories
articles.author: Stephan Blum, Research Associate, Institute for Prehistory and Early History and Medieval Archaeology, University of Tübingen
paras: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticised for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer” at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.
On October 23, the platform posted the first seven minutes.

As archaeologists and art historians, we’re not here to review the film for its artistic quality or even its historic accuracy. Instead, we’re here to point out the real problem with the whole endeavour: the promise of historical accuracy failed before the first frame was even rendered.

Contrary to what many of you might assume, as historians we think Musk’s underlying idea – bringing together everything archaeology and history have to offer and using AI as a tool to explore and work with that knowledge – is a genuinely exciting one. We see considerable potential in that approach: a system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar can hold in mind, such as how ceramic styles spread. The problem is turning that into a film that claims to be historically accurate.
Any attempt to produce a complete, coherent visual narrative would inevitably require AI to go beyond the evidence and invent what we do not know.

Archaeology is inevitably working with a fragmentary record: only a tiny proportion of the past survives in the ground, and only a fraction of that is ever excavated. For instance, open the boxes in the Troy depot and you’ll find spindle whorls and loom weights; however, you won’t find the cloth they made. Everyone at Troy wore textiles but the textiles are gone.

So, like the textiles, everything that cannot be recovered directly from the archaeological record has to be interpreted and explained through hypotheses, however well-founded they may be scientifically. There will always be gaps, uncertainties and competing interpretations.
AI, by design, would inevitably fill these gaps.

Suppose Grok Imagine was given everything the Troy Project holds: a century and a half of excavation, thousands of plans, pottery drawings and photographs, plus the small-finds catalogue. It would generate connections, details and entire scenarios where the historical and archaeological evidence offers no firm answers.
Generative AI is built to produce complete images, even when there are visible gaps. These gaps are often filled with influence from other existing media like film sets, games, paintings.

This is precisely where the problem lies: additions by AI may be plausible, even convincing. Some sceptical reviewers concede that some of those seven minutes pass for real. But convincing is not accurate, and the space between the two is where archaeology lives.

The Odyssey is also an interesting target for accuracy. It’s a poor witness to the past: shaped centuries after the palaces its about fell, it is a palimpsest of Mycenaean memory and iron age worldview – not a snapshot. Odysseus, Helen and Circe are not people archaeology could confirm. However, there is a lot of creative media about the world these characters are believed to have inhabited.

Back to those textiles. A model trained on that record would inherit our ignorance along with our knowledge. It will hallucinate or imagine because it must paint every pixel. It will draw on all the evidence, media and more connected to the themes and history to render a finished cloak, dyed and draped. This rendering will look like a convincingly accurate garment where the honest research answer is “fibre known, colour unknown”.
What survives is not what happened

None of this makes AI useless. A system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar could see – such as how ceramic styles spread. But every such pattern would first be a pattern in the record, not a picture of the past.

A genuinely archaeological AI would do what generative AI rarely does: show its uncertainty as clearly as its confidence. Take armour. Only fragments survive at Troy. Where evidence permits several reconstructions, it would show several rather than present one confident, definitive option. Where only fragments survive, it would show only the fragments. And where the evidence runs out, it would say so, clearly marking what is documented, what is inferred and what is merely plausible.

This approach to rendering possibilities is close to what the London Charter (2009) and the Seville Principles (2011), two international guidelines for virtual reconstructions of heritage, have long demanded: transparency rather than smoothing.

Which world gets reconstructed is also a choice. Troy spans phases centuries apart, and Mycenaean palaces differed from Hittite cities: there is no single “bronze age”. The record can support a conflict at Troy; it cannot establish Homer’s Trojan war as one event. However, an AI model picks one Troy and never mentions the choice.

The film will likely be forgotten within a news cycle or two; what remains is the method. The most accurate Odyssey would not be the most definitive or confident one; it would end where we began: on the boxes of whorls and weights, and the empty space where the cloth should be.
Historical accuracy does not mean filling every gap. It means showing where the gaps are.

articles.title: Four ways thinking like a strategist can make you a better padel player
articles.author: Veselina Stoyanova, Associate Professor in Strategy & International Management, University of Birmingham
paras: As an avid tennis player, I never imagined an injury would lead me to discover a new sport. But just a few months ago, forced to take a break from tennis, I picked up a padel racket for the first time. I assumed that years of playing tennis would give me a head start; after all, how different could two racket sports really be? To my surprise, the answer was “very.”

Padel, which originated in Mexico in the late 1960s, is an enclosed-court racket sport typically played in doubles. Combining elements of squash and tennis, it uses solid, stringless bats, lower-compression balls and glass or mesh walls off which the ball can rebound. While it has long been a sporting obsession in Spain and Latin America, its explosive global growth has recently made it the fastest-growing racket sport worldwide.

While tennis and padel share many technical similarities, they require somewhat different ways of thinking. I soon discovered that some of my tennis instincts were actually holding me back. Hitting harder wasn’t always the answer. Attacking too early often left me exposed, while patience, positioning, and anticipating my opponents’ next move proved far more valuable than a powerful shot.

That experience made me curious about something beyond court technique. As a researcher in strategic management, I focus on how people and organisations navigate uncertainty, allocate limited resources and make decisions to gain a competitive advantage. I quickly began to recognise these exact same challenges on the padel court.

What if, I wondered, the secret to becoming a better padel player isn’t simply learning to hit the ball better, but learning to think more strategically? Here are four ways thinking like a strategist can help you level up your padel game:
1. Consider yourself a resource orchestrator, not a player

According to resource orchestration theory, which emphasises how managers organise, combine and deploy resources to create value, success depends not simply on the resources you possess, but on how effectively you orchestrate them.

We can apply this directly to padel. For example, if your partner has an exceptional volley, try to create opportunities for them to use it. Before starting a match, discuss your individual strengths with your partner and plan how best to combine them. In fact, what you initially view as a resource constraint can often be turned to your advantage.
2. Train your attention, not just your shots

In both business and padel, your strategic mindset starts with where you focus your attention. The real power of training your attention is cumulative. During each game, choose one specific aspect to focus on closely: whether that is your opponents’ bandeja (a defensive overhead shot) or their footwork and movement.
After several games, your observations will accumulate into strategic insight. This accumulated knowledge allows you to anticipate your opponents’ moves rather than simply react to them.
3. Play the opponent in front of you, not the one in your head
To increase your odds of winning, try to reflect on and challenge your assumptions about your opponents and how you judge their moves on the padel court.

We often rely on first impressions about competitors, which can distort our judgement and affect our play and decisions. Instead, view your assumptions as hypotheses to be tested based on your opponents’ next shots, rather than as concrete truth.
4. Thinking backwards can lead you further forward
Instead of trying to assume your opponents’ next move, practice backward reasoning.
Imagine a situation where your opponents are dominating the net. Try not to assume their next move, but to influence the choices they make next.

To develop a strategic mindset and improve your padel practice, define your desired outcome and work backwards, identifying the decisions that will help you achieve it. Strategic management means that, rather than simply reacting to your opponents’ next moves, you actively consider how your own actions can influence their next shot.

To play strategically, stop asking yourself “Where should I hit the ball next?” and start asking “What position do I want to be in two shots from now, and how can my next shot help me get there?” By thinking backward from the outcome you want to create, you transition from reactive play to tactical planning.

For instance, if your opponents are dominating the net, your immediate goal isn’t to hit an instant winner, but to force them out of their attacking position. Hitting a soft drop or deep lob buys you time, surrenders their net advantage and sets up a favourable position to control the point on your next turn.

To become a better player in padel, tennis, or any racket sport, the smartest way to win a point is often to out-think rather than out-play your opponent. Next time you’re on the court, remember that your strategic mindset is a skill you can train – just like your forehand, volley, or bandeja.

articles.title: The John Lewis Christmas ad captures the deep need for grandmothers
articles.author: Helen Minnis, Professor of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Glasgow
paras: Like many of us, I always enjoy the John Lewis Christmas advert and 2026 is no different. This year, I love the fact that the star of the show is a grandmother.

Feeling disconnected from her visiting grandchildren and ready to resort to cash in envelopes for Christmas, Gloria (Kristin Scott Thomas) is scolded by her childhood toy dog Pickles, who comes to life and whisks her on a whirlwind London TukTuk ride. Inspired, Gloria transforms her home office into a glittering, disco-lit “gran cave”, bridging the generation gap by sharing her sense of wonder with her grandchildren.

We can’t all have grandmothers as chic as Gloria, but many of us were lucky enough to have grans who loved us just as much — and we probably took them as much for granted. I suspect many grans feel like an old-fashioned back boiler, half-invisible in the background, but warming the family without anyone noticing. Sociologists often refer to this as “kinkeeping”: the often unacknowledged emotional and practical groundwork that holds intergenerational families together, but is all too easily taken for granted.

Those grandparents lucky enough to see their grandchildren on a regular basis, and who get to be involved socially and emotionally in their lives, feel less lonely and tend to live healthier lives. Sadly though, many feel devalued by the younger generation.

Gran’s alliance with Pickles helps her to rediscover the real Gloria. The person who can lean her head back into the headrest of a fantasy shocking-pink super-chariot, and feel the wind in her hair as it whizzes her through the Christmas fairy-lit streets. The Gloria that is silly enough to spend her Christmas savings on glittery spangles. The Gloria that hasn’t forgotten how to dance. This is the gran that the children love.

This year’s John Lewis ad is a reminder that families are not just made up of mum, dad and 2.4 children. Humans are different from many of our ape cousins. We are “cooperative breeders”. This means we tend to have children in quick succession and, because human babies are unusually dependent compared to other baby apes, parents need help from other adults.

Across evolution, it seems that human parents drew in the help of “alloparents” – most often grandmothers but also grandfathers, aunties, uncles and cousins – to help with childcare. This was wonderful for the human species as children learned from a wide range of fascinating adults.

In many parts of the world, children live every day of the year surrounded by family members who can lift the load off parents and take their share of bringing up the kids. But the John Lewis advert is a reminder that many British families are nuclear. In these families, children grow up separated from grandparents, so that grans and granddads are left trying to reach out and create a Christmas relationship that in other parts of the world they might have all year round.

Research has shown that grandmothers can help reduce the risk of mothers getting depressed after a new baby is born; that having a gran living in the home can reduce the chances of a child needing to go to casualty after an accident; that grandmothers who help with childcare are good for children’s mental health and development.

Every year, festive ads tap into something we clearly miss: the chaotic, comforting warmth of a bigger family circle. Modern routines and long distances often leave grandparents sidelined until the holidays roll around. Yet as the science shows, being closely involved in each other’s lives protects grandparents against isolation and helps kids flourish.

Finding ways to keep that spark alive beyond December means more than finding the perfect presents. It’s about making room for the shared laughter, silliness and connection that both generations actually thrive on.

articles.title: What makes music truly ‘Russian’? The forgotten debate between Tchaikovsky and his star pupil
articles.author: Stacy Olive Jarvis, PhD Candidate in in Musicology, University of Birmingham
paras: What makes a piece of music Russian? A folk tune, a church melody, or simply the fact that the composer was born in Russia? For 19th-century composer Sergei Taneyev (1856-1915), the answer was complicated. He wanted Russian composers to develop a musical voice of their own. But he believed they could do so by learning from composers elsewhere in Europe.

By the time Taneyev began his career, the world of classical music in Russia was expanding. Musical life, which had previously been centred on the imperial court and aristocratic families, increasingly came to include public concerts and new institutions for training professional musicians. Conservatoires opened in St Petersburg in 1862 and in Moscow in 1866, where teaching methods developed in various European countries were employed.

However, musicians’ views on how the Russian tradition should develop differed. Tchaikovsky was one of the first graduates of the St Petersburg Conservatoire. At the same time, a group known as “The Five” – César Cui, Aleksandr Borodin, Mily Balakirev, Modest Mussorgsky and Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov – drew on folk songs, Russian history and folk legends in their quest to forge a distinctive national style.
The question at stake was how Russian composers could create their own tradition while drawing on established European musical culture.

November 2026 marks 170 years since Taneyev’s birth. This anniversary offers a chance to revisit an argument with his former teacher, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840-1893), over a question that still shapes how we listen: how much does a national identity label actually tell us about music?

Taneyev was closely connected to some of the best-known names in Russian classical music. He studied with Tchaikovsky, later taught Rachmaninoff and Scriabin, and directed the Moscow Conservatory between 1885 and 1889.

In my research on Tchaikovsky’s operas, I have explored how his music brought Saint Petersburg to life as a Russian city shaped by European culture. In his opera Eugene Onegin (based on the novel by Alexander Pushkin), elegant ballroom dances evoke the capital’s aristocratic society, contrasting with the rural world of the earlier scenes.
But Tchaikovsky and Taneyev argued over how drawing on European traditions could help composers develop a distinctively Russian voice.

Taneyev was troubled by the direction Russian music might take. He thought composers needed to do more than place Russian folk tunes inside the kinds of pieces already familiar from European concert halls.
Instead, they should examine how earlier European composers had turned folk songs and church melodies into complex works. Could Russian musicians do something similar with their own songs?

That meant studying counterpoint: the art of combining different melodies so that each remains distinct while working with the others. Bach was an important model. For Taneyev, learning these techniques could help a composer create music with a recognisably Russian character.

Education was part of the plan. Taneyev argued that Russian songs should become a foundation of musical training. Composers would learn their craft through melodies connected to their own surroundings, while drawing on knowledge built up elsewhere.
Tchaikovsky was sceptical. In their 1880 correspondence, he questioned whether Russian music could be separated from European music in the way his pupil proposed.
Taneyev explained his position through an image. European music was a tree that had grown over centuries from folk and church melodies. Russian melodies were seeds from which another tree might grow.

Russian composers therefore had a choice. They could help the existing European tree grow, or cultivate something of their own. Crucially, Taneyev did not want musicians to turn their backs on Europe. Its history could show them how to proceed. Studying another culture’s achievements could help them develop their own.

Tchaikovsky challenged the comparison. Why treat European music as a single tree? French, German and Italian music already had different characters. He preferred to imagine a garden, with Russian music growing alongside its neighbours.

For Tchaikovsky, music could belong to a wider European culture and still sound distinctly Russian. He heard French qualities in the music of Massenet and Bizet, just as Taneyev heard Russian qualities in Tchaikovsky’s compositions. Neither man was arguing that national character meant nothing. They disagreed about how it developed, and whether composers needed a deliberate programme of study to create it.

Tchaikovsky’s argument also had limitations. His letter dismissed English and Spanish music in terms that revealed his own prejudices. His garden was not a place where every tradition received equal admiration. Nevertheless, Tchaichovsky rejected the idea that Russian music needed to grow outside Europe. It had already taken root in shared musical ground.
Taneyev’s life shows how those connections worked in practice. In 1876, he reported playing Tchaikovsky’s piano concerto at the Paris home of the French composer Camille Saint-Saëns.

Tchaikovsky subsequently asked him to discuss a possible concert of his music in Paris. Taneyev would play the piano; French contacts would help make it happen. The plan came to nothing, but the correspondence shows musicians working across borders to find listeners.

The exchange was artistic as well as practical. Taneyev’s 1884 cantata John of Damascus, for choir and orchestra, draws on Russian sacred music while using the techniques he studied in earlier European works.

For listeners, the important point is that these influences could coexist. Learning from another tradition did not automatically make a composer’s music less connected to home. Calling Taneyev Russian remains useful. It connects him to the language, institutions and experiences that shaped his life. But it cannot explain his music on its own.
His career suggests that Russian classical music was never a closed national tradition. Even the ambition to create something distinctly Russian could depend on knowledge acquired from elsewhere.
That matters when composers become symbols of national identity today. Their music can express a sense of belonging while carrying the traces of other places, people and ideas.
Taneyev and Tchaikovsky disagreed about the best way forward. But argument points towards a shared lesson: that a national musical voice could emerge through international exchange.
